Thanks for looking into it @arw2019. When using `axis=1`, you want to specify which columns to group, rather than using something like `df.groupby('B', dropna=True, axis=1)`. Here is an example:

```
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [0, 0, 7, 1], "B": [1, 2, 4, 3]}, index=list('abcd'))
gb = df.groupby([1, np.nan], dropna=True, axis=1)
result = gb.transform('sum')
```

This errors out in the same way master does, in `_set_result_index_ordered`.  I think all that needs to be done is to do the same operation you're adding for `axis=0`, but on the columns instead:

    result.columns = self._selected_obj.columns[result.columns]

I haven't tested this thoroughly though, and am okay with doing in a followup.

issue_context.title: BUG: DataFrameGroupBy.__getitem__ fails to propagate dropna=True
issue_context.body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [x] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

xref #35014 

Creating a separate issue as the `dropna=True` requires a different fix to `dropna=False`  (resolved by #35078)

#### Problem description

The setup is:
``` python
In [1]: import pandas as pd                                                                                                                    
In [2]: df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [0, 0, 1, None], "B": [1, 2, 3, None]})                                                                        
In [3]: gb = df.groupby("A", dropna=True)                                                                                                      
```
All three of these commands:
``` python
In [4]: gb['B'].transform(len)                                                                                                                 
In [5]: gb[['B']].transform(len)                                                                                                               
In [6]: gb.transform(len)                                                                                                                      
```

review_comments: can we just *always* use this formulation? e.g. just use the if clause regardless here?

well I mean for axis==0; also I think this is incorrect for axis==1 (though it likley won't trigger the if clause).

can you refactor to do this?

> can we just _always_ use this formulation? e.g. just use the if clause regardless here?

We can but the slice will drop some attributes (for example frequency for a datetime index - we have testcase which won't quite roundtrip if we do this). Will change as long as you're ok with that

> well I mean for axis==0; also I think this is incorrect for axis==1 (though it likley won't trigger the if clause).

Right because for `axis=1` we don't drop rows.

FTR we don't fully support/test the `axis=1` case atm. I'll do that in a follow-on once this is in

> well I mean for axis==0; also I think this is incorrect for axis==1 (though it likley won't trigger the if clause).
> 
> can you refactor to do this?

On second thought I don't think we can 

AFAIK if we don't drop rows then we keep the original index which isn't an indexer into the original object's index. When we drop rows we reindex with an integer index (and that's a valid argument to `__getitem__`). So the case of no rows dropped doesn't fall through the slice and I think we do have to treat those two cases separately here
We only want to remove this line when going through _set_result_index_ordered above. Instead, move it to the else clause a few lines up.
so the else clause is when we're returning an empty object (for a non-empty result we pass through _set_result_index_ordered)

this is really hard to understand why you are doing this. 

`.dropna` should modify the `.result_index` on the Grouper object no?

you mean the if condition or what we're doing inside the if? 

we have the if because AFAIK `result` has a simple index when `_set_result_index_ordered` is initally called and we need to restore the original index  if it's non-standard or a mulitiindex

If no rows were dropped `set_axis` does the job, but `set_axis` throws in case of shape mismatch between `result.index` and original index 

since `result.index` is a standard index we can get labels of the dropped object by using `result.index` to slice the original index. In the OP it's amounts to doing:
```
In [24]: df.index   # original index                                                                                                                                                                                         
Out[24]: Index(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], dtype='object')

In [26]: df.index = df.index[[0, 1, 3]]    # index of dropped object                                                                                                                                                                
    ...: df.index                                                                                                                                                                                                 
Out[29]: Index(['a', 'b', 'd'], dtype='object') 
```
`self.axis` does not propagate correctly rn so checking that does nothing atm
